@O/<Football Skills>@
Terms for the many skills in football.
A few of them appear in the Training
menu during the game.

@O/<Attacking Skills>@
Skills needed to take goals from the
opposition. They matter most for
FWs and attacking MFs.

@O/<Overhead Kick>@
Kicking the ball over your own head,
with your body fully off the ground.
Also called a bicycle kick.

@O/<Shooting>@
Kicking the ball at the opposing goal.
Many kinds exist: instep and inside
shots, volleys struck from the air and
headed shots.

@O/<Set Piece>@
Restarting play with a dead ball.
Restarts include free kicks and corner
kicks. In the game, you can pick the
kickers before the match starts.

@O/<Diving Header>@
Diving to head a ball that is low
to the ground. Often seen when
clearing or shooting in front of goal.

@0/<Trivela>@
Literally "three toes". The usual name
for a shot hit with the outside of the
foot, off the base of the three outer
toes, so that it bends outwards.

@0/<Banana Shot>@
A nickname, used in Japan, for a shot
with curl. Depending on the player's
skill, it may bend, or bend and dip,
in many different ways.

@O/<Heading>@
Playing a ball in the air with your
head. It is a staple of aerial duels,
and tall players are often good at it,
but smaller players can still win the
ball with good body use and timing.

@O/<Support Skills>@
Moving into a position where a
teammate with the ball can be sure of
finding you with a pass. This gives
the player on the ball more options.
Every position needs it, but it is
especially vital for the MFs who turn
defence into attack.

@O/<Assist>@
A pass that leads directly to a goal.
Players with many assists have had a
hand in more goals.

@O/<Early Cross>@
A cross whipped into the box early,
from just past the halfway line, before
the defence is set. The opposition must
scramble to react, so it is a dangerous
pass that often leads to goals.

@O/<Wall Pass>@
A player who receives the ball returns
it first time to the passer, as if it
bounced off a wall. Also known as the
One-Two Pass.

@O/<Wedge Pass>@
A linking pass into the feet of a
teammate standing in the middle of an
organised defence. It draws the
defenders' attention to the centre, so
it is also a decoy pass that lets the
attack develop from there.

@O/<Cruyff Turn>@
A feint made famous by the Dutchman
Johan Cruyff. You fake a shot or cross
to draw the defender in, then pull the
ball behind your standing foot, turn
and leave the defender wrong-footed.

@O/<Ground Pass>@
A pass rolled along the ground.

@O/<Switch of Play>@
Sending the ball to the opposite side,
where the defence is thin, to change
the flow of attack. Using the whole
pitch can reveal gaps in the defence,
but it must be done with quick passing
or the ball may be intercepted.

@O/<Through Ball>@
A pass played in behind the back line.
It often leads to a goal. As it goes
behind the line, a receiver who runs
too early will be caught offside. The
timing between passer and receiver is
what matters most.

@O/<Cross>@
Sending the ball into the box from the
wing. The more accurate it is, the
more likely it is to lead to a goal.

@O/<Forward Pass>@
A pass towards the opposition's half.

@O/<Passing Triangle>@
Two players support the player on the
ball by forming a triangle with them.
This gives at least two passing lanes,
so the player on the ball has more
options.

@O/<Ball Control>@
Controlling a moving ball with any part
of the body bar the arms. Players who
are good at it can move on to their
next action more quickly.

@O/<Dribbling>@
Carrying the ball forward under control
with the feet. Players from South
America are especially good at it, and
a skilled one is known as a dribbler.

@O/<No-Look Pass>@
A pass made without looking at the
teammate it is meant for. Hard for the
opposition to read.

@O/<Passing>@
Giving the ball to another player.
There are many types, such as short
passes, long passes, through balls and
one-twos.
A player who is especially good at it
is sometimes called a "passer".

@O/<Feint>@
A move meant to fool an opponent.
Used to dribble past an opponent, or to
shake off a marker in front of goal.

@O/<Positioning>@
Adjusting your position on the pitch.
By reading the play and correcting it
constantly, you stay ready for the next
action.

@O/<One-Two Pass>@
A player who receives the ball returns
it first time to the passer, as if it
bounced off a wall. Also known as the
Wall Pass.

@O/<Defensive Skills>@
Skills for stopping the opposition's
attack and preventing shots. Mainly
needed by DFs and defensive MFs.

@O/<Interception>@
Cutting out a pass, or winning the ball
from an opponent who is dribbling or in
the middle of controlling it.

@O/<Overlap>@
A defender or midfielder running past a
teammate on the ball to join the attack
in the opposition half.

@O/<Covering>@
Making up for a teammate's mistake. For
example, when a DF is beaten by a FW,
another player takes over marking that
forward.

@O/<Zonal Marking>@
A way of defending in which each player
is given a set zone. Any opponent who
enters the zone is marked by the player
in charge, whether or not they have the
ball.

@O/<Tackling>@
Trying to win the ball from the player
who has it. Includes slide tackles and
shoulder charges.

@O/<Closing Down>@
Chasing down the opponent who has the
ball in their half. It is the first
step of defending.

@O/<Charging>@
A type of tackle in which you hit an
opponent's shoulder with your own. Also
called a shoulder charge.

@O/<Defending>@
Refers to players who defend, or to the
act of defending. Defenders are shown
as DF in the game.

@O/<Defensive Line>@
Seeing the DFs' positions as a line.
Pushing the line up shrinks the area
in which the opposition can play.

@O/<Pass Cut-Off>@
Cutting out a pass between opposition
players. Sometimes also called an
interception.

@O/<Man-to-Man Marking>@
A style of defending in which a player
marks a specific opponent one-on-one.
DFs often mark the opposition's striker
this way. Also known as man marking.

@O/<Long Ball>@
Sending a long pass from your own half
towards the opposition's half. Used to
turn defence into attack in one go, or
to save time getting the ball upfield.
It is usually hit with the instep, the
top of the foot, which gives the most
power.

@O/<Forcing One Side>@
Closing off the passing and dribbling
routes of the player on the ball, to
herd them towards one side. A defensive
technique.

@O/<Goalkeeping Skills>@
Skills for stopping shots taken by the
opposition's attack. They are skills
used only by goalkeepers.

@O/<Organising>@
Shouting instructions to teammates.
Goalkeepers often do this to organise
the defence.

@O/<Throwing>@
One way to start an attack once the
ball is caught. There are three types,
underarm, sidearm and overarm, used as
needed.

@O/<Deflecting>@
When the ball arrives with no time to
spare, using the palm to change the
ball's path.

@O/<Rushing Out>@
How a goalkeeper comes out to deal with
crosses from the wing and balls played
behind the defensive line.

@O/<Drop Kick>@
Kicking the ball with the instep as it
bounces. It travels furthest, but is
less accurate as a result.

@O/<Punt>@
A goalkeeper dropping the ball from the
hands and kicking it before it hits the
ground.

@O/<Rolling Down>@
Putting weight on the ball-side leg and
falling sideways. Used when there is no
time to spare, such as against a low
shot along the ground.

@O/<Kickers>@
Players who take free kicks, corners,
and penalties. In the game, you can
choose a kicker for each type of kick.

@O/<Penalty Kick>@
A kick from the penalty spot, aimed
directly at goal. Everyone except the
opposing goalkeeper and the kicker must
stay out of the penalty area.

@O/<Indirect Free Kick>@
A way of restarting play: a free kick
from which a goal only counts if the
ball touches another player first.

@O/<Corner Kick>@
A kick given to the attacking side when
the ball goes over the goal line off a
defender. It is taken from the corner
arc.

@O/<Goal Kick>@
Awarded to the defending side when the
ball, last touched by an attacker, goes
over the goal line. The kick is taken
from inside the goal area.

@O/<Direct Free Kick>@
A way of restarting play: a free kick
from which the ball can go straight
into the goal.

@O/<Free Kick>@
A kick awarded for an opposition foul,
taken with no pressure. Defenders must
stay 10 yards away. There are two
types: direct and indirect.

@O/<Place Kick>@
A kick awarded for an opposition foul,
taken with no pressure. The defenders
must stay 10 yards from the kicker.
It covers free kicks and corner kicks.

@O/<Crossbar>@
The goal's horizontal bar, 2.44 metres
above the ground. It can be no thicker
than 0.12 metres.

@O/<Corner Arc>@
The area inside a quarter circle of
radius 0.915 metres drawn at the corner
of the goal line and touchline.

@O/<Corner Flag Post>@
The flagpole standing at each corner,
with a blunt tip. It must be at least
1.5 metres tall.

@O/<Goalpost>@
The upright posts of the goal. They are
set 7.32 metres apart, and may be no
wider than 0.12 metres.

@O/<Goalmouth>@
The opening of the goal: 2.44 metres
high and 7.32 metres wide. It is
sometimes called "the frame".

@O/<Flanks>@
The longer lines of the pitch are the
touchlines. The area close to those
lines is called the flank.

@O/<Space>@
An area of the pitch. Making good use
of open space, where the defence is
thin, helps you gain the upper hand in
a match.

@O/<Centre Circle>@
The circle of 9.15 metres radius
drawn from the midpoint of the halfway
line.

@O/<Halfway Line>@
The line dividing the pitch into two
equal halves. It joins the two
touchlines.

@O/<Penalty Area>@
The area in front of goal that includes
the goal area, measuring 16.5 metres by
40.32 metres. Inside it, the goalkeeper
is allowed to use their hands.

@O/<Formation>@
The way players are arranged on the
pitch. Teams use many different ones.
It normally shows how the ten outfield
players line up, giving the numbers of
DFs, MFs and FWs from left to right.

@O/<3-4-3>@
A formation of 3 DFs, 4 MFs and 3 FWs.
A strong front line makes it an
attacking formation.

@O/<3-5-2>@
A formation of 3 DFs, 5 MFs and 2 FWs.
An attacking formation that makes use
of wing-backs.

@O/<3-6-1>@
A formation of 3 DFs, 6 MFs and 1 FW.
It is the 3-5-2 with a FW dropped back
into midfield. There is plenty of open
space up front, so choose it when you
want to exploit that.

@O/<4-3-3>@
A formation of 4 DFs, 3 MFs and 3 FWs.
A very attacking formation with three
forwards.

@O/<4-4-2>@
A formation of 4 DFs, 4 MFs and 2 FWs.
Balanced between attack and defence, it
is among the most orthodox formations.

@O/<4-5-1>@
A formation of 4 DFs, 5 MFs and 1 FW.
It is the 4-4-2 with one FW pulled back
to a deeper position. There is plenty
of open space up front, so choose it
when you want to exploit that.

@O/<5-3-2>@
A formation of 5 DFs, 3 MFs and 2 FWs.
A more defensive version of 3-5-2. It
keeps things tight at the back and is
well suited to wing counter-attacks.

@O/<5-4-1>@
A formation of 5 DFs, 4 MFs and 1 FW.
The focus is on defence, packing the
area in front of goal. Counter-attacks
after winning the ball are how the
team attacks.

@O/<Tactics>@
The team's game plan. Types include
hold-up play, left and right side
attacks, a central breakthrough and
counter-attacks, used as needed.

@O/<Post Play>@
Play that acts as a wedge, mainly near
the opposing goal. The player holds the
ball until team-mates arrive, then
passes to them. A player who is good at
this is called a Target Man.

@O/<Left Side Attack>@
An attack down the left touchline, for
example by sending the ball into the
box from the flank.

@O/<Right Side Attack>@
An attack down the right touchline, for
example by sending the ball into the
box from the flank.

@O/<Down the Middle>@
Breaking through the centre, the
shortest route to the opposing goal, to
score. To get through the most heavily
defended area, it needs many players
with strong individual skill.

@O/<Counter-Attack>@
Let the opposition attack, win the
ball, then strike before their defence
is organised and score.

@O/<Offside Trap>@
All the defenders push up together,
raising the line to leave opposing
players in offside positions.
It requires forcing the opposition into
forward passes only, with the defence
stepping up just before the pass is
made. Team unity is the key here.

@O/<Midfield Defence>@
How midfielders defend in the centre
of the pitch. Options are Zonal Press
and Normal.

@O/<Zonal Press>@
A tactic of pressing hard on the
opponent with the ball, limiting their
passing lanes and winning it back.

@O/<Defensive Line>@
The defenders line up and push forward
together, shrinking the space the
opposition attackers can move in and
making it easier to play them offside.

@O/<Libero>@
Italian for "free man". A centre-back
who usually sits behind the defensive
line as a sweeper but joins the attack
when the moment is right, creating
chances.

@O/<Sweeper>@
Plays in the middle of the defensive
line with no man to mark, covering for
the whole defence.
A system with a sweeper behind the
defensive line is called a sweeper
system. It means "one who cleans up".

@O/<U22 (Under-22)>@
Players aged 22 or under. Some events
restrict who may enter, and this age
limit can be one of the conditions.

@O/<U23 (Under-23)>@
Players aged 23 or under.
For the same reason as U22, some
competitions include this in their
entry conditions.
World Sports Festival qualifiers are
special: under the regulations only
players aged 22 or under may play.

@O/<Points System>@
A win in 90 minutes earns 3 points, a
win by V-Goal earns 2 points and a draw
earns 1 point. The team with the most
points in each stage wins the title.

@O/<Official Matches>@
Matches that go on record. In this game
they mainly refer to
J1 First Stage
J1 Second Stage
and J2 matches.

@O/<J1>@
The top league in Japan. It currently
has 16 clubs and uses a points system.
The year is split into early and late
stages, and the results decide the
final table. Every year the bottom 2
clubs swap places with the top 2 teams
in J2.

@O/<J2>@
The league one level below J1. In
Sakatsuku it has 14 clubs, who compete
over a year on a points system to
decide the final standings.
Every year the top 2 clubs swap places
with the bottom 2 teams in J1.

@O/<Stage>@
In J1 the year is split into an early
and a late half. The early half is
called the First Stage and the late
half is the Second Stage. Each stage
is a single round-robin league.

@O/<Senior National Team>@
A country's national side, also called
the A team or full team.
There is no age limit.
In Brazil it is called the "Selecao".
In Italy it is called the "Azzurri",
after the blue of its kit.

@O/<Second Stage>@
The late stage of the year in J1.
Every J1 club plays each other club
once in a round-robin.

@O/<Championship>@
Played between the First Stage winners
and the Second Stage winners to decide
the national champions for that year.
It is not held if the same team wins
both the First and Second Stages.

@O/<Division>@
A measure of a league's strength within
the country, as in J1, J2 and the JFL.
J1 and J2 together make up the
J.League.

@O/<Knockout>@
A way of running a competition where a
win takes you into the next match. The
team left standing at the end becomes
champion. It is often used in cups.

@O/<Penalty Shoot-Out>@
If it is level after extra time, both
sides take penalties in turn with 5
kickers each. It ends as soon as the
result is decided. If still level after
5 each, one more kicker each follows
until a winner emerges. It is used in
knockouts that must produce a winner.

@O/<First Stage>@
The early stage of the year in J1.
Every J1 club plays each other club
once in a round-robin.

@O/<Home Match>@
A match in your club's home town.
The home side is normally considered to
have the advantage. A match between
clubs that share a home town is called
a "derby match".

@O/<V-Goal>@
Extra time of 15 minutes each half, in
which the match ends as soon as either
team scores.
It is called the "Golden Goal" at the
World Cup.

@O/<Playing Style>@
The kind of play a player is best at.
Some are good dribblers, some are good
passers, and some are good at joining
the attack up front. Players come with
all sorts of playing styles.

@O/<Wing-Back>@
Sometimes written WB.
A defender whose main job is to run up
the open space on the flank and put in
crosses.

@O/<Playmaker>@
Also called the "brains" of the team.
A player who can read the flow of the
match and build the attack.

@O/<Goalkeeper>@
The only player allowed to use hands,
inside the penalty area. They can also
play outside it, as long as they do not
use their hands. Goalkeepers also have
longer careers than players in other
positions.

@O/<Full-Back>@
Sometimes written FB.
A defender who covers the flank.
They are defenders but also join the
attack, for example by overlapping.

@O/<Stopper>@
A centre-back who marks the opposing
forward and literally stops the
opposition attack. That is why they are
called stoppers.

@O/<Centre-Back>@
Sometimes written CB.
A defender who plays in the centre.
They can be divided further into
sweepers and stoppers.

@O/<Up Front>@
A player at the very front of attack.
One player there is a "lone striker"
and two are a "strike partnership".

@O/<Dribbler>@
A player who is good at dribbling.
Many players from South America are
especially good at it.

@O/<Target Man>@
A player who acts as a wedge near the
opposing goal. They hold the ball until
team-mates arrive, then pass to them,
and so start the attack.

@O/<Holding Midfielder>@
In Portuguese this means 'steering
wheel'. This player steers the match in
attack and defence. Using two of them
in a formation is a "double pivot".

@O/<Libero>@
Italian for "free man". A centre-back
who normally sits behind the defensive
line as a sweeper, but who goes forward
into the opposition half when the time
is right to create chances.

@O/<Positions>@
The position is where a player plays
on the pitch and the role they have in
a match. There are four positions:
FW: mainly attacks
MF: attacks and defends
DF: mainly defends
GK: stops the opposition's shots

@O/<FW>@
Short for "forward".
A player whose main role is to join the
attack and score using shots, headers
and so on.

@O/<MF>@
Short for "midfielder".
A player who plays around the middle of
the pitch. Also called "midfield" or
"half".

@O/<Defensive MF>@
A midfielder who focuses on defence.
Also called a defensive half or
a holding midfielder.

@O/<DF (Defender)>@
Read as "defender".
A player who defends, mainly near their
own goal, to keep the opposition attack
away from it.

@O/<Full-Back>@
A defender who covers the flank.
As well as defending, they have an
attacking role and join attacks,
for example by overlapping.

@O/<Centre-Back>@
A defender who plays in the centre.
They can be divided further into
sweepers and stoppers.

@O/<Goalkeeper>@
The only player allowed to use hands,
inside the penalty area. They can also
play outside it, as long as they do not
use their hands. Goalkeepers also have
longer careers than players in other
positions.

@O/<Out of Play>@
When the ball in play goes completely
over a line (goal line or touchline) or
the referee stops play, the ball is out
of play. Anything played then is void,
and a goal scored then does not count.

@O/<Advantage>@
When the referee decides that stopping
play for a foul would put the fouled
team at a disadvantage, play is allowed
to continue despite the foul.

@O/<Own Goal>@
Putting the ball into your own goal by
mistake. In this case the goal is
awarded to the opposition.

@O/<Offside>@
A player in the opposing half and ahead
of the ball may not play unless 2 or
more opponents are between them and the
goal line. If there is only 1 opponent
and they interfere with play, it is an
offside offence, and the defending side
is given an indirect free kick.

@O/<Kick-Off>@
Starting the match, or restarting it
after a goal, by kicking the ball from
the centre spot into the other half.

@O/<Caution>@
A sanction the referee gives a player
for repeated fouls or unsporting acts.
The referee shows a yellow card then.

@O/<Coin Toss>@
A way to decide, before the match,
which ball the match starts with.
The team that calls heads or tails
correctly can choose to kick off or
choose which end to play.

@O/<Referee>@
The official with authority over how
the match is run, who enforces the
rules and makes the final decisions.

@O/<Throw-In>@
How play restarts after the ball goes
out over the touchline. The ball is
thrown in with both hands from where it
went out.

@O/<Substitutions>@
In official matches, up to 3 players
may be substituted.
However, the referee must be told the
names of the substitutes before the
match begins.
In the J.League, from 2001 a fourth
substitute is allowed if the match goes
into extra time.

@O/<Sending-Off>@
A sanction the referee gives a player
for a particularly malicious offence.
A second caution in one match also
means a sending-off. The referee shows
a red card to tell the player.
A sent-off player cannot play in the
next match either.

@O/<Half-Time>@
The break between the first and second
halves. It normally lasts 15 minutes at
most, unless the referee allows more.
You can change tactics and make
substitutions during this time.

@O/<Back-Pass>@
When a teammate deliberately kicks the
ball to the goalkeeper. If the keeper
handles a ball kicked by a teammate, it
is an offence, even in the penalty
area. However, if the pass is made with
anything other than the foot, handling
it is not an offence.

@O/<Handling>@
Playing the ball with a hand or arm.
It is an offence in football and the
other side is awarded a direct free
kick. A goalkeeper who uses hands or
arms outside the penalty area also
commits an offence.

@O/<Assistant Referees>@
The two officials who help the referee
run the match. One is on the main stand
touchline and the other on the opposite
touchline.

@O/<Stoppage Time>@
Time wasted during a match for reasons
unconnected with play. The referee adds
that time to the end of the match.

@O/<Attackers>@
Players who join the attack and score.
This is mainly the job of forwards and
attacking midfielders.

@O/<Captain>@
The leader of the team.
The captain commands the players and
holds everyone together.
A captain with strong leadership will
lift team morale and help players show
their usual form.

@O/<Aerial Duels>@
Contesting a ball that is in the air.

@O/<Clubhouse>@
A facility next to the club's training
ground, used for things like players'
weight training.
In the game, enlarging the clubhouse
makes training go more smoothly.

@O/<Finishing>@
How often shots turn into goals.
"High finishing" means a player is
strong when chances come.

@O/<Condition>@
A player's state before a match.
It gives a guide to how much of their
ability they can show.

@O/<Ginga>@
A feint from the Brazilian martial art
capoeira. The skill of moving the body
to bewilder an opponent so that they
cannot read your movement is called the
forerunner of Brazilian football.

@O/<Starting XI>@
The 11 players who start the match.
The 5 players on the bench are called
substitutes. A trump card among them is
sometimes called a "super sub".

@O/<Stadium>@
The ground where matches are played.
In the game, enlarging the stadium
lets you draw bigger crowds.

@O/<Stamina>@
Physical strength.
When stamina falls, work rate and
concentration drop and a player cannot
play normally.

@O/<Midfield>@
Players who play around the middle of
the pitch. Sometimes called "half" or
"MF".

@O/<Nutmeg>@
Playing it between an opponent's legs.

@O/<High Ball>@
A ball that goes high into the air.
Contesting high balls often leads to
aerial duels.

@O/<Pass and Go>@
After passing, sprinting straight
forward without stopping.
The basis of individual tactics.

@O/<Pitch>@
The area of the stadium where the
match is actually played.
Also called the field.

@O/<Physical Training>@
Training to build physical fitness.

@O/<Brazilian Exercises>@
Exercises Brazilian footballers use for
warm-ups before matches and so on.
Steps, trunk twists and other movements
are done rhythmically.

@O/<Free>@
When nobody is marking a player and
they can move freely. Passing to a free
player opens up chances.

@O/<Malicia>@
A Portuguese word meaning "cunning".
In football it means the tricks and
mind games of a match.

@O/<Man of the Match>@
The best player in the match.

@O/<Youth>@
A team made up of young players.

@K/<Your First Training Session>@
When you train for the first time, try
leaving the menu to your manager. They
should build the club's training menu
following their policy. Once you are
used to it, try changing the menu
yourself. Also, until you learn how
easily players tire or get injured,
avoid hard training and rest often.

@K/<How Training Works>@
Basically, set up team training and
now and then check growth progress or
add a rest day. That is all you need.
If a player has an ability you want to
develop, set individual training for
part or all of their menu.

@K/<Using Team Training>@
The club's basic training. Team
training alone can develop every
ability. Build the menu to match the
club's basic policy.

@K/<Using Individual Training>@
Individual training is done separately
from the team menu. Use it to improve
a player who needs particular work, to
let young players who rarely play and
are not tired train on rest days, or to
give easily tired players extra rest.

@K/<Developing Forwards>@
First, teach the basics of a forward
through position training. Then train
to suit the playing style you want.
In technique, it is a good idea to work
on speed and heading as well as
shooting.

@K/<Developing Attacking MFs>@
Attacking MFs come in many types, so
do not just develop them evenly. Decide
what type you want and train for it.
Each player also has strengths and
weaknesses. Listen to the coach's words
and spot their traits. For technique,
work on passing and ball retention.

@K/<Developing Defensive MFs>@
Defensive MFs link defence and attack.
On defence, train interceptions to stop
opposition attacks early. For attack,
train passing and strength.
Defensive MFs also need more running
than any other position, so build up
their endurance well.

@K/<Developing Full-Backs>@
Full-backs must do more than defend:
they must run up the flank to join
attacks when chances arise. Train
tackling and interceptions, of course,
but also dribbling and running speed.

@K/<Developing Centre-Backs>@
Centre-backs are the key to defence.
Train tackling and interceptions
thoroughly.
Then choose libero or stopper training
depending on whether you want an
attacking libero or a player who simply
guards the area in front of goal.

@K/<Developing Goalkeepers>@
Teach the basics of goalkeeping with
position training.
Then work on shot-stopping and rushing
out.
Also remember to practise passing so
they can kick accurately upfield.

@K/<Raising Condition>@
Each player's condition rises and falls
on a different cycle. Some training can
speed up or slow down these changes.
In particular, special conditioning
restores condition sharply. However, it
causes heavy fatigue, so it cannot be
overused. Be careful.

@K/<Recovering from Fatigue>@
Fatigue is recovered by resting from
training or by not playing in matches.
Give players with a lot of fatigue an
emergency rest day from training.

@K/<How Much Rest Is Needed>@
How easily players tire varies from
player to player. Resting several days
in a row also rests the body more.
Give each player rest that suits how
easily they tire. When you build the
team training menu, schedule a rest day
at least once a month to avoid injury.

@K/<Raising Teamwork>@
Group training from the team menu
slowly raises teamwork. Playing matches
together raises it too. Also, setting
teamwork training on the same day in
individual training lets you focus on
building teamwork between the chosen
players.

@K/<When a Player Is Injured>@
There are two kinds of injury, serious
and minor. A player with a minor injury
can train and play, but try not to use
them if you can. Forcing a player with
a minor injury can lead to a serious
one or, at worst, a career-ending one.
It is vital to rest them until fully
recovered.

@K/<Training Effectively>@
Over the long term, it is better to
build up fitness and skill while they
are young.
Training while fatigued is not very
effective either. When fatigue is
high, do not push players; plenty of
rest is what matters.

@K/<Using Special Conditioning>@
Sometimes, such as in a title decider
or against a strong side, you will want
players to be in good condition.
In that case, give special conditioning
to players with poor condition.
However, it adds a lot of fatigue, so
avoid using it on players who are
already very tired.

@K/<Using Emergency Rest>@
Players who tire easily may not fully
recover on the rest days set for the
rest of the squad. In that case, set
an emergency rest just for them, to
suit how tired they are.
Emergency rest leaves the training
menu unchanged, so there's no need to
edit the menu afterwards.

@K/<Choosing Set-Piece Takers>@
Let the club's best dead-ball player
take free kicks. Corners work the same
way, but if that player is a threat in
front of goal and strong in the air,
it can pay to let someone else take
them. For penalties, pick a player who
shoots well and never gets rattled.
Ask the coach what they think.

@K/<Changing Positions>@
In position-based training, a player
trains according to the position
currently assigned to them. So if you
want different training, you'll need
to change that player's position.
Some players can have their position
changed at the start of each year.

@K/<Do Managers Make a Difference?>@
The manager runs training on the
ground, and the closer it is to their
favourite style, the more efficient
it is, so players develop faster.
Preferred tactics, formations and
styles vary between managers. When
signing one, check that their style
matches the direction you want.

@K/<When Stamina Runs Out Quickly>@
A player's stamina in a match depends
on their endurance and how much they
run. Tiredness also makes stamina
go faster. If players keep running
out of steam, watch their fatigue and
build up their endurance. Ability
drops sharply once stamina is gone, so
timely substitutions matter too.

@K/<Position Players by Their Colour?>@
A player's colour shows their best
position, or the one set at the start
of the year. So if they're also good
elsewhere, they can shine there too.
You can ask about a player's best
positions in the meeting room.

@K/<Effects of Study Abroad>@
Study abroad develops players more
than normal training. Growth isn't
uniform, though: which abilities
improve depends on the destination.
Younger players and those on the rise
learn the most overseas, so think
carefully about when to send them.

@K/<Effects of Overseas Camps>@
At an overseas camp, players are
coached by local instructors. As with
study abroad, the effects depend on
the destination.

@K/<How Long Do Players Keep Growing?>@
Growth varies from player to player,
so there's no general answer. Some
improve a lot early on, while others
develop late. Each ability has its
own potential, so some abilities may
stop improving even while the player
is still developing.

@K/<When Injuries Are Frequent>@
If players seem tired, give them more
rest. The state of the training ground
also affects injury risk. Grass is
naturally kinder to players than dirt,
and a rough pitch means more injuries.
So keep an eye on the training
ground too.

@K/<Choosing a Captain>@
Ask the players what they think. Pick
someone who seems confident. Bear in
mind that squad morale differs
depending on whether the captain is
playing or on the bench. So, from the
confident players, try to choose one
who is likely to be a regular starter.

@K/<Choosing a Formation>@
Every formation has its pros and cons,
so none is simply the best. Choose
freely. Pick one that suits your
tactics and your squad. Players also
have their strengths and weaknesses,
so if tactical understanding stalls,
be bold and switch tactics.

@K/<Choosing FW and MF Setups>@
Choose to suit players' abilities.
Even in the same position, players
differ in ability and favoured play:
a passing FW and a shooting FW, or an
attacking MF and a defensive MF.
In matches, it can also help to adapt
to the opposition's line-up and the
tactics you choose.

@K/<Building a Defensive Club>@
Generally, placing more players nearer
your own goal makes the club more
defensive. Even players in the same
position differ in defensive
awareness, so try to have as many
defensive-minded players as possible.
Defensive awareness can be raised to
some extent with defensive training.

@K/<Building an Attacking Club>@
Generally, placing more players nearer
the opposition goal makes the club
more attacking. Even players in the
same position differ in attacking
awareness, so try to have as many
attack-minded players as possible.
Attacking awareness can be raised to
some extent with attacking training.

@K/<What Is Play Style?>@
Play style in individual training is
the type of behaviour a player shows.
Think about each player's role in
matches and train them accordingly.

@K/<Making the Right Side Attack Work>@
Improve tactical understanding of the
Right Side Attack, and place players
with the right abilities for side
attacks on the right flank.

@K/<Making the Left Side Attack Work>@
Improve tactical understanding of the
Left Side Attack, and place players
with the right abilities for side
attacks on the left flank.

@K/<Making Central Breakthrough Work>@
Improve understanding of Central
Breakthrough tactics, and place
players with the abilities it needs in
central positions.

@K/<Making the Counter-Attack Work>@
Improve understanding of the
Counter-Attack, and play suited
players up front.

@K/<Making Hold-up Play Work>@
Improve tactical understanding of
Hold-up Play, and place players with
the right abilities in the FW roles.

@K/<Making the Offside Trap Work>@
Improve tactical understanding of the
Offside Trap, and place players with
the right abilities in defence.

@K/<Making the Zonal Press Work>@
Improve tactical understanding of the
Zonal Press, and make sure every
player has the abilities it needs.

@K/<Who Suits the Right Side Attack>@
The Right Side Attack is when the
right-sided players push forward. So
it helps to place a quick, skilful
dribbler on the right. Also train
passing so that final balls succeed
more often, which makes it even more
effective.

@K/<Who Suits the Left Side Attack>@
The Left Side Attack is when the
left-sided players push forward. So
it helps to place a quick, skilful
dribbler on the left. Also train
passing so that final balls succeed
more often, which makes it even more
effective.

@K/<Who Suits Central Breakthrough>@
Central Breakthrough drives through
the opposition from in front of goal.
Place good dribblers and passers in
central positions.

@K/<Who Suits the Counter-Attack>@
The Counter-Attack means striking
quickly the moment you win the ball.
Place FWs who are fast and clinical
enough not to waste chances.

@K/<Who Suits Hold-up Play>@
Hold-up Play is when an FW receives
the ball up front, holds it or lays it
off, and so creates chances. Place FWs
who are strong in the air and in
challenges.

@K/<Who Suits the Offside Trap>@
The Offside Trap needs the whole
defensive line to act as one. Everyone
must understand the tactic, of course,
but the defenders also need to work
together and have a leader to command
the line. So place players with strong
leadership in defence.

@K/<Who Suits the Zonal Press>@
In the Zonal Press, everyone from the
forwards to the defenders keeps
pressuring the opposition to win the
ball. It naturally uses more stamina.
So as well as improving understanding
of the Zonal Press, you need players
with good endurance.

@K/<Effects of the Zonal Press>@
The Zonal Press uses more stamina than
usual. But once understanding grows,
you can win the ball in midfield and
snuff out the opposition's chances
early. It is an advanced tactic,
though: if it is poorly mastered it
can backfire and put you under
pressure, so be careful.

@K/<Effects of the Offside Trap>@
Catching the opposition's passes
offside can stop their attacks. But if
the defenders' understanding or
communication is poor, the opposition
can get in behind the line, leaving
their FW one-on-one with your GK, so
be careful.

@K/<Is Any Tactic Better?>@
You can't say which tactic is the
strongest. Each has its pros and
cons. Effectiveness rises when you
understand a tactic properly and put
the most suitable players in place.

selection on the same screen. The

flag, are paired, so choosing one also

transport and football popularity.

Here you can maintain the grounds,

and build extra training grounds.

more effective.

Here you can rebuild the stadium and
add or remove facilities that can be

This command rebuilds the current
Clubhouse. Rebuilding it increases the
space for facilities.

Add facilities to the Clubhouse or

space for it in the Clubhouse.

This command rebuilds the current
stadium. Rebuilding it increases the
space for facilities and also raises
the maximum number of spectators.
From Level 5, you cannot rebuild until
the town has developed to some extent.

@Y/<Add or Remove Facilities>@
Add facilities to the stadium, or
remove ones you have added.
Adding a facility needs enough free
space for it in the stadium.
Removing a facility frees its space.

@Y/<Roof Installation>@
You can install a roof on the stadium.
A roof reduces the drop in attendance
compared with having no roof.
It is vital in rainy places.

@Y/<Facility Maintenance>@
Maintain the training ground, replace
the turf, install lights and more.
Well-equipped, well-kept grounds mean
fewer injuries in training and make
training more effective.

@Y/<Extra Training Ground>@
You can add a second training ground,
making two in total. The extra room
makes training more effective.

Clubhouse. You can mainly check each

@Y/<Add Stadium Facilities>@

one you add reduces the stadium's
remaining space on screen by its size.
Free space is shown in "blue" and
space in use in "red".

@Y/<Remove Stadium Facilities>@
Remove facilities currently installed
in the stadium. Each one you remove
adds its size to the free space shown.
Free space is shown in "blue" and
space in use in "red".

@Y/<View Stadium Facilities>@

@Y/<Condition>@

@Y/<Re-turf (Long)>@
Lay long grass on the ground. Training

@Y/<Re-turf (Short)>@
Lay short grass on the ground.

ground and injuries are less likely,
though not as much as with long grass.
The condition also gets worse less
easily, so it is very good value.

@Y/<Choosing Lights>@
You can install lights at a ground.

can train for longer. Each ground can
have one set of lights.

the trend in income and expenditure for

current population, transport, land

transport, land prices and football
popularity rose or fell since last
month.

be kept.

be kept.

conditions and impose penalties if

the club. Choose between the total
invested this month and the total
invested since the club was founded.

month.

the local "economic climate", which

housing. More housing raises the local
"population", which means more

enthusiasm for sport. More enthusiasm
improves local athletic ability and

links. Better transport brings bigger
crowds to home matches, and it also

Draw up a training menu for your
players. Menus are planned one month at
a time: once set, the same pattern is
repeated every month until changed.

@Y/<Change Strategy>@
Change player positions and choose the
club's "formation", "tactic",
"midfield defence" and "Defence Type".
You can also choose set-piece takers.

@Y/<Run Training>@
Carry out the menu you created.

much each player has improved.

@Y/<View Teamwork>@
See how well the Starting XI players
link up with those around them. White
lines mean good, red lines very good.

@Y/<Manager's Assessment>@
Ask the manager for an overall rating
of the club, with feedback and advice
on tactics and Defence Type.

@Y/<Team Training>@
Set the training menu for the whole
team. Every player follows the policy
you set. You can also pick "Leave it
to the Manager" and have a menu drawn
up in line with the manager's policy.

@Y/<Individual Training>@
Set a training menu for each player.

to their policy. Press the Y Button to
apply individual training to everyone;
press again to restore the previous
settings.

@Y/<Special Rest>@
Choose players to rest from this turn's
training. Even if a menu is set, they
will not train this turn.

@Y/<Special Conditioning>@
Special conditioning raises condition
greatly. It is useful before a match
you absolutely must win this turn, but
fatigue rises sharply too, so watch
fatigue closely.

@Y/<Player Positions>@
Change players' positions in a match.
Players at the right of the screen are
substitutes who can replace Starting XI
players during the match.

each formation you can rearrange the
FW and MF in a variety of orders. You
can change it again at half time, or
during play by selecting
"Change Plan".

Choose the tactic for the match. Here,
tactic means your attacking approach.
You can change it again at half time,
or during play by selecting "Change
Plan".

@Y/<Midfield Defence>@
Midfield defence is a choice of whether
to use the Zonal Press. The Zonal Press
uses more stamina, but if the players
understand it well enough, midfield
defence is stronger than normal.

You can change it again at half time,
or during play by selecting
"Change Plan".

Players train however they like. What
they do depends on each player's
personality.

Training to improve understanding of

Training to improve understanding of
the 4-3-3 formation. Players will be

Training to improve understanding of

Training to improve understanding of

Striker, Dribbler, Playmaker, Holding
Midfielder, Full-back, Stopper, Libero
and Goalkeeper.

Trains one specific skill intensively.
There are 10 in all: Shooting,
Heading, Dribbling, Passing, Tackling,
Interceptions, GK Shot-Stopping, GK
Rushing Out, Set-Piece Kicks and
Penalties.

@Y/<Fitness>@
Training for the foundations of each
player's athletic ability. There are 3
kinds: Strength, Speed and Endurance
Training.

@Y/<Rest>@
Only selected players rest to recover
from built-up fatigue. The other
players do the training assigned.

@Y/<Free Training>@
Players train however they like. Each
trains to play better in the
position they are best at.

@Y/<Shooting>@
Improves your finishing in training.
Players will be able to score not just
from clear chances but from difficult
situations too.

@Y/<Heading>@
Training to improve finishing with the
head. Players will be able to score
from high balls sent into a crowded
goalmouth.

@Y/<Passing>@
Training to improve passing skill.
Players will link up well in attack and
be able to play passes that lead to
goals.

@Y/<Tackling>@
Training for more powerful tackles.
Players will pressure the opposition
attack heavily and be able to shut it
down.

@Y/<Interceptions>@
Training to improve interception rate.
Players will stop the opposition's
attacks and get more of their own.

@Y/<GK Shot-Stopping>@
Training to improve the goalkeeper's
shot-stopping. Players will reliably
save the opposition's shots.

@Y/<GK Rushing Out>@
Training to sharpen the goalkeeper's
timing and judgement in rushing out.
Players will snuff out chances such
as crosses.

@Y/<Set-Piece Kicks>@
Training to improve set-piece kick
accuracy. Players will be able to play
passes from free kicks and corners
that create goal chances.

@Y/<Penalties>@
Training to improve finishing from the
penalty spot. Under enormous pressure,
players will calmly put the ball in
the net.

@Y/<Speed Training>@
Make a chosen player train to build
explosive speed. They will be able to
give everything in a split-second
chance.

@Y/<Endurance Training>@
Make a chosen player train to build
endurance. They will build a body that
doesn't tire over a full match.

@Y/<Strength Training>@
Make a chosen player train to build
strength. This boosts tackle power and
shooting power.

@Y/<3-6-1>@
Changes the match formation to 3-6-1.
If it works well, expect tremendous
ball control in midfield.

@Y/<5-4-1>@
Changes the match formation to 5-4-1.
It suits the counter-attack. If it
works well, you can launch counters
that leave the opposition's defence
behind.

@Y/<3-5-2>@
Changes the match formation to 3-5-2.
If it works well, you can switch
quickly between attack and defence and
play a match with no weaknesses.

@Y/<4-4-2>@
Changes the match formation to 4-4-2.
It adapts flexibly to both attack and
defence, making for solid matches.

@Y/<5-3-2>@
Changes the match formation to 5-3-2.
If it works well, expect a solid
defence that gives the opposition no
goals. With so few in midfield, it's
best to pair it with a tactic that
uses the full-backs well in attack.

@Y/<3-4-3>@
Changes the match formation to 3-4-3.
If it works well, expect high
scoring power.

@Y/<4-3-3>@
Changes the match formation to 4-3-3.
If it works well, it becomes a
formation that is strong in both attack
and defence.

@Y/<4-5-1>@
Changes the match formation to 4-5-1.
If it works well, expect a very solid
defence and a quick transition from
defence to attack.

@Y/<Hold-up Play>@
Changes the match tactic to hold-up
play. If it works well, attacks near
goal become more varied and scoring
power rises.

@Y/<Left Side Attack>@
Changes the match tactic to the left
side attack. If it works well, you can
exploit the space down the left and
build attacks from there.

@Y/<Right Side Attack>@
Changes the match tactic to the right
side attack. If it works well, you can
exploit the space down the right and
build attacks from there.

@Y/<Central Breakthrough>@
Changes the match tactic to central
breakthrough. If it works well, you can
drive straight down the shortest route
to goal.

@Y/<Counter-Attack>@
Changes the match tactic to the
counter-attack. If it works well, you
can strike fast from a solid defence
and score before the opposition get
back.

@Y/<Zonal Press>@
Changes the match midfield defence to
the Zonal Press. If it works well, you
can win the ball in midfield by
crowding the opposition, then move
into attack.

@Y/<Normal>@
Changes the match midfield defence to
Normal. Without the Zonal Press,
midfielders use less stamina.

@Y/<Line>@
Changes the Defence Type used in
matches to Line. If it works well, the
defensive line pushes up all at once to
catch the opposition offside.

@Y/<Libero>@
Changes the Defence Type used in
matches to Libero. If you have a
suitable player, they join the attack
at the right moment, so expect more
attacking power.

@Y/<Sweeper>@
Changes the Defence Type used in
matches to Sweeper. With a suitable
player, they cover gaps in defence
precisely, so expect a defence with
no weaknesses.

@Y/<Penalties>@
Choose who takes penalties in matches.
A player with good finishing and the
nerve to handle pressure is the ideal
taker.

@Y/[FK]@
Choose who takes free kicks in
matches. Pick a player with accurate
kicking, one who can aim straight at
goal even from very awkward spots.

@Y/[CK]@
Choose who takes corners in matches.
Pick a player accurate enough to put
the ball where teammates can score,
even in a crowded box.

the next. If a match is scheduled this

town. In the home town you can use
training and local menus that the
office does not offer.

Handle staffing for our club here:
hiring and releasing players, managers
and scouts. You can also ask scouts to
look for players you want.

View all kinds of data about our club
here. It falls into four groups:
schedule, club info, match record and
player rankings.

sets the tournament format, match
format and number of teams below
automatically. Choose from four:

format chosen in Quick Select.

cannot be changed.

or "Under 23".

enter the tournament: "J.League",

Registers a Free Player saved on your
VMU to your Dream Club. After
selecting this, the load screen
appears. Choose the Free Player to
register from the VMU.

Pick players to register to your Dream
Club from preset clubs. After
selecting this, choose "Overseas
Players" or "Domestic Players", then
the club of the player you want to
register.

Load a Dream Club file saved earlier
to register or remove players again.
The load screen appears after
selecting this. Choose the Dream Club
file to load from your VMU.

Saves your Dream Club to a VMU. The
save screen appears after selecting
this. Choose the VMU to save to.

Check the players registered to the
Dream Club you are building. After
selecting this, a list of registered
players appears. Move the cursor to a
player and press the B Button to
unregister them.

Finishes building the Dream Club and
returns to the title. Returning erases
the Dream Club data you are working
on, so save to your VMU before you go
back.

Choose the "Versus Club" you want to
take into Challenge Mode from your
VMU. Only a "Versus Club" can be used
in Challenge Mode.

Choose the rank you want to challenge.
Naturally, the higher the rank, the
stronger the clubs you face. You start
at 10-kyu, but if another club has
progressed before, you can freely
choose up to the dan that club
reached.

to the network, then goes straight to
the Sakatsuku website. To connect,
your network registration must be
complete and your provider must be the
Sega provider.

Plays back a LIVE file downloaded from
the network tournament page,
recreating the match results. The
results may differ slightly from those
posted online.

funds. Move the cursor with Up/Down
and press the Confirm button on an
item to see more detail.

month. Home attendance changes with
our popularity, ticket price,
advertising budget, supporter numbers,
match importance, weather and more.

this month. Home match ratings change
with our popularity, match profile,
advertising budget, TV coverage,
supporter numbers and more. Ratings
also affect which sponsors appear.

Supporters' Club members. Supporter
numbers rise and fall with membership
fees, advertising, popularity and this
month's results. They in turn affect
attendance, TV ratings and Supporters'
Club commands.

around the world this month. Transfers
are listed by newsworthiness. Many
more moves happen than the ones shown,
so it's a handy guide to the players
out there.

this month. It affects attendance:
high prices keep crowds away, low
prices bring them in. The ticket price
options can grow or shrink as the club
develops.

Decide this month's club advertising
spend. It affects recognition, which
in turn affects supporter numbers,
popularity and match attendance. The
options can grow or shrink as the club
develops.

popularity trend, the change in
supporter numbers, and the average and
highest TV ratings of all home
matches.

this year, with the placing in each
tournament they entered.

@Y/[Personnel News]@
Selects 30 of the main personnel moves
worldwide this year. A guide to how
much movement there has been, and to
how good the players are.

@Y/[Home Town Data]@
Shows how much your home town has
grown this year, with data such as
population, transport level and land
prices.

@Y/[Sponsorship Deals]@
Choose the sponsors, such as
companies, who provide the club with
funds. You can sign up to 10 sponsors
for one to five years. Some sponsors
attach conditions and penalise you if
they are not met, so be careful.

@Y/[Negotiate]@
Negotiate directly with each player.
Offer a length and amount, guessing
what the player wants. An offer too
close to the limit can leave a player
unhappy. Meeting the player's demands
as far as possible should avoid any
big failures.

@Y/[Leave It to Secretary]@
Leave all contracts to the secretary.
It often costs more than negotiating
yourself, but players are treated
carefully so they stay content. The
biggest plus is the saved effort. You
can hand over partway through.

@Y/[Don't Renew]@
Tells just this player their contract
will not be renewed. After marking
unwanted players, you can leave the
rest to the secretary.

@Y/[End Negotiations]@
Ends contract renewal talks. Any
player whose contract is not yet
renewed is treated as "Don't Renew".

@Y/[Negotiation Screen]@
The player first states how many years
they want, and you reply. Then enter a
salary. Players have their own wishes,
so some get angry at the years or
amount you enter. Upsetting players is
unwise in the long run.

@Y/[Change Player Position]@
Change a player's position. The coach
first suggests positions, and you
choose from those. Suggestions are
based on past training and results, so
you can also train a player for the
position you want using training
menus.

@Y/[Select Player]@
Select the player you want to make an
offer to and enter terms, based on the
player's wishes and the scout's
advice. Other clubs chase high-profile
players, so you will need high terms.
New players are added every turn, and
strong ones may appear later.

@Y/[Make Offer]@
Offer a contract length and salary.
Unlike signing through Personnel, you
basically get one try, but if no other
club signs the player you may get
another chance. For a player you want,
offering extra in case other clubs
move in is a good strategy.

@Y/[Schedule]@
Check this month's schedule. In J2 you
can freely choose a tournament in
February only; in J1, in February and
November. The tournaments offered
change with your results, last year's
results and the years played.

@Y/[Sign Players]@
Sign Japanese and foreign players.
Make an offer to players your scouts
have listed, and sign them if you
agree terms. You can also set a
position, or send a scout to search by
name and region. The list updates
early in Weeks 1 and 3 of each month.

@Y/[Study Abroad]@
Send club players to study abroad.
Destinations vary with the club's
situation, partnered cities, the
manager's origin and the home town.
Destinations overlap with the Overseas
Camp in February.

@Y/[Transfer]@
Transfer club players away. A forced
transfer to another club removes them
from your squad. Use it when you want
another player but the squad is full.
Careless transfers can hurt the
players left at the club.

@Y/[Change Manager]@
Change the current manager. The list
updates at the start of each month. As
with players, managers appear
according to the club's record and
years, so good ones may not turn up
early on. Each has favourite systems,
tactics and training policies.

@Y/[Change Scout]@
Change the current scout. The list
updates at the start of each month. As
with players and managers, scouts
appear according to the club's record
and years, so good ones may not turn
up early on.

@Y/[Sign Domestic Players]@
Sign Japanese players. The quality and
number on the list depend on your
current scout. Depending on the club's
record, years and current manager,
some players refuse the scout's
approach and do not appear. The list
updates early in Weeks 1 and 3.

@Y/[Sign Overseas Players]@
Sign foreign players. The quality and
number on the list depend on your
current scout. A scout from the
player's home country makes them
appear more easily, but the club's
record, years or manager may still
keep them off. Updates early in Weeks
1 and 3.

@Y/[Set Position]@
Tell your scout the positions you
need, and only matching players are
listed. Scouts have favourite
positions, and narrowing the search
means fewer players than usual.
Changes take effect from the next list
update.

@Y/[Search by Name]@
Name a player and choose a region, and
your scout can search for that one
player. Depending on the club's
situation or the scout's ability, you
may be unable to negotiate even after
a find. A search takes time, and you
cannot sign others meanwhile.

@Y/[Sign Free Player]@
Sign a player saved as a data file
with Create Data in the Quit/Settings
screen. There is no negotiation,
unlike other signings. Free Players
cannot be saved to file again and are
barred from some online tournaments,
so use them only as temporary helpers.

@Y/[Player Negotiation]@
The player first states how many years
they want, and you reply. Then enter a
salary. Players have their own wishes,
so some get angry at the years or
amount you enter, and complain even
after joining. You can negotiate
salary up to three times.

@Y/[Player Negotiation]@
The player first states how many years
they want, and you reply. Then enter a
salary. Players have their own wishes,
so some get angry at the years or
amount you enter, and complain even
after joining. You can negotiate
salary up to three times.

@Y/[Set Position Screen]@
Narrow down the positions of the
players your scout lists. Your choice
takes effect at the next scout list
update and stays in force until you
change it. Narrowing the search
naturally means fewer players.

@Y/[Search by Name Screen]@
Send a scout to search for one
specific player. Entering a region is
not required, but it takes longer
without one. A partial name is
accepted, but may bring back an
unintended player, or a different
player with a similar name.

@Y/[Study Abroad Screen]@
Send a player to study abroad for six
months, one year or two years. A
player can go only once in a lifetime.
Choose a destination that suits their
ability, or they return without
improving. Destinations vary with the
club and home town.

@Y/[Transfer Screen]@
Transfer club players to other clubs.
When the 16-player squad is full and
you want another player, transfer
someone to free a space. Too many
careless transfers can unsettle the
players who remain.

@Y/[Change Manager Screen]@
Change the current manager. Each
manager has favourite tactics and
systems. The best choice is one who
suits the club's current policy, or
the direction you want to take later.
Managers have personalities, and some
players just don't get on with them.

@Y/[Change Scout Screen]@
Change the current scout. Scouts have
specialist areas, shown on screen. S
is best, followed by A, B and C. Some
players can only be signed by certain
scouts, especially foreigners, who
tend to be linked by home country.

@Y/[Weaknesses]@
Players tell you what they feel is
their weakest area. Only players with
something to say speak, so those you
can't select feel no weakness. You can
also check injuries and slumps here.

@Y/[Selling Points]@
Players tell you their selling points.
Players who feel they have none say
nothing. You can also hear about good
news here.

@Y/[Complaints]@
Hear what each player is unhappy
about. Players with no complaints say
nothing. Listening often can sometimes
resolve their complaints.

@Y/[Opinion on Club]@
Ask the manager for opinions on the
club's situation. You learn suitable
policies and which positions or squad
depth are lacking. Opinions here may
also reflect the manager's favoured
policies.

@Y/[Set Title]@
Give a chant a title. Up to 10
full-width characters can be entered,
and the title appears on the chant
selection screen.

@Y/[Time Signature]@
Choose three or four beats to the bar.
It has no other effect, so pick the
one that suits your song.

@Y/[Tempo]@
Choose the tempo from nine levels. The
default is the middle one, level 5, so
set it to make the song slower or
faster.

@Y/[Load]@
Load saved data or songs prepared
within Sakatsuku. You can edit those
songs too, so a good way to learn the
controls at first is to pick one as a
model.

@Y/[Save]@
Save the chant you composed. Save
files made here can be attached to
e-mail, or passed to friends by
connecting VMUs and swapping files.

@Y/[Quit]@
Ends composing. If you quit without
saving, your song data will be lost.
To erase everything you have written
so far, select this and enter again to
reset the score.

@Y/[Compose]@
Compose chants for the club or Japan
National Team. It is a normal score,
so you can enter sheet music almost
exactly as written. The number of
chants available to the club grows as
supporter numbers increase.

@Y/[Create Face]@
Create a player's face. Choose which
part to change, then choose a part
type. Some parts also let you subtly
change the position or shape.

@Y/[Strong Foot]@
Set the Edit Player's stronger foot.
Left and right make no difference to
ability.

@Y/[Auto]@
Automatically sets any items not yet
decided. The face currently shown is
used.

@Y/[Origin]@
Choose the player's home country or
prefecture. Choosing a foreign country
uses a foreign player slot on joining,
so take care. Origin slightly affects
ability.

@Y/[Ability]@
Choose a position and its linked
traits to set the player's ability.
Traits come in three types: strengths,
personality and special skills. The
combination sets basic ability.

@Y/[Quit]@
Ends editing the player. Any blanks
are filled in automatically. A club
cannot have two Edit Players at once.
Even if you sign one through Anywhere
Sakatsuku, the club's existing one is
deleted on loading, so be careful.

@Y/[Supporters' Club Screen]@
Supporters rank your club's players by
their impressions, and you can ask for
their views on stadium facilities.
Once certain conditions are met, you
can compose and set the club's chants.
In some cases you can set one for
Japan too.

@Y/[Supporter Rankings]@
Supporters are surveyed about club
players, giving an indirect view of
each player's impression and traits.
Votes and comparisons with other
players show how memorable each one
is to supporters, which helps with
training and team selection.

@Y/[Ask Opinions]@
Ask supporters for views on stadium
facilities. More supporters means more
people attending, so requests
inevitably grow. They start as
requests but grow into demands if
ignored, and built-up discontent hurts
membership and popularity.

@Y/[Ranking Screen]@
Choose the survey topics for
supporters. Some hidden topics appear
depending on the club's players. The
survey's reliability rises and falls
with supporter numbers and discontent,
but can be estimated from the votes.

@Y/[Set Policy]@
Set the Youth Team's policy, to
develop players with an eye on the
future. For strength now, follow the
club's current policy. To plan ahead,
give orders based on future tactics,
including a younger squad. Starting
young also builds physique well.

@Y/[Assign Mentor]@
Assign a first-team player as a mentor
to a Youth player. The mentor must be
over 30. It can backfire if they don't
get on, but the youngster inherits
some of the mentor's ability, allowing
successor-style development.

@Y/[Coach Assessment]@
Coaches describe each Youth player's
traits: preferred tactics and systems,
plus ability by position, with
comments.

@Y/[Formation]@
Choose the Youth Team's formation
training policy. Youth players train
to suit the formation chosen.

@Y/[Tactics]@
Choose the Youth Team's tactics
training policy. Youth players train
to suit the tactic chosen.

@Y/[Midfield Defence]@
Choose the Youth Team's midfield
defence training policy: use the Zonal
Press or not. Youth players train to
suit the choice.

@Y/[DF Type]@
Choose the Youth Team's DF type
training policy. Youth players train
to suit the DF type chosen.

@Y/[3-6-1]@
The Youth Team trains to suit a 3-6-1
formation. If it works well, expect
great ball control in midfield.

@Y/[4-5-1]@
The Youth Team trains to suit a 4-5-1
formation. If it works well, expect a
very solid defence and quick
transitions from defence to attack.

@Y/[5-4-1]@
The Youth Team trains to suit a 5-4-1
formation. It suits the
counter-attack: if it works well, they
can counter and leave the opposition
defence behind.

@Y/[3-5-2]@
The Youth Team trains to suit a 3-5-2
formation. If it works well, they
switch between attack and defence
quickly and play without a weak
moment.

@Y/[4-4-2]@
The Youth Team trains to suit a 4-4-2
formation. It handles attack and
defence flexibly, making for solid
matches.

@Y/[5-3-2]@
The Youth Team trains to suit a 5-3-2
formation. If it works well, expect a
solid defence that never lets the
opposition score. With few
midfielders, use tactics that make
good use of the full-backs in attack.

@Y/[4-3-3]@
The Youth Team trains to suit a 4-3-3
formation. If it works well, it is
excellent in attack and defence.

@Y/[3-4-3]@
The Youth Team trains to suit a 3-4-3
formation. If it works well, expect a
high goal-scoring ability.

@Y/[Hold-up Play]@
The Youth Team trains to suit Hold-up
Play tactics. If it works well,
attacks around the goal become more
varied and scoring improves.

@Y/[Left Side Attack]@
The Youth Team trains to suit Left
Side Attack tactics. If it works well,
they exploit space down the left to
build attacks.

@Y/<Right Flank Attack>@
The Youth Team will train to adapt to
the right flank attack tactic. If it
works, they can exploit the space on
the right and build their attacks.

@Y/<Central Attack>@
The Youth Team will train to adapt to
attacking through the middle. If it
works, they can take the shortest
route to goal.

@Y/<Counter-Attack>@
The Youth Team will train to adapt to
the counter-attack tactic. If it
works, a solid defence lets them hit
quickly and score before opponents get
back.

@Y/<Normal>@
The Youth Team will train to adapt to
normal midfield defence. With no zonal
press, midfielders tire less quickly.

@Y/<Zonal Press>@
The Youth Team will train to adapt to
the zonal press in midfield. If it
works, they can crowd out opponents,
win the ball and launch an attack.

@Y/<Line>@
The Youth Team will train to adapt to
the Line defender type. If it works,
they can push the defensive line up at
once and catch opponents offside.

@Y/<Libero>@
The Youth Team will train to adapt to
the Libero defender type. If a suitable
player is there, they will join the
attack at the right moment, so expect
more attacking power.

@Y/<Sweeper>@
The Youth Team will train to adapt to
the Sweeper type. If the squad has a
suitable Sweeper, they will cover gaps
in defence accurately and keep things
very tight at the back.

@Y/<BGM>@
Listen to the music used in this game.
Select with Left/Right and press the
A Button to start a track.

@Y/<SE>@
Listen to the sound effects used in
this game. Select with Left/Right and
press the A Button to start playback.

@Y/<Finish>@
End the month-end report and go on to
the next month. Once you finish, the
reports for that month cannot be viewed
again, so please be careful.

@Y/<Finish>@
End the year-end report and go on to
the next year. Once you finish, the
reports for that year cannot be viewed
again, so please be careful.

@Y/<Choose Secretary>@
Choose a secretary. Each has different
likes and personalities, but all have
the same ability. Use the introductions
to pick your favourite. They will teach
you a lot about running the club.

@Y/<Rival Club>@
This club was founded at the same time
as yours, so its strength is closest
to yours. Your results against them
may show how well you run your club.

@Y/<Compose>@
Go to the score and write a song. Move
the cursor with Up/Down/Left/Right and
press the A Button on the score to add
notes, or on the rhythm row to add
rhythm. If a vowel is selected at top
right, supporters will sing along with
the notes on the score. Press the B
Button to play your song back.

@Y/<Chant Editor>@
Compose a chant. Set the five vowels
A, I, U, E and O to make it sound as if
it is really being sung.
Use the sample songs you can pick from
Load as a guide.

@Y/<Assign Club Chant>@
Choose the chant for your club from the
songs in your save data or the samples
provided. The data you choose is stored
in the club data, so you do not need to
keep a separate chant file. Please note
that opposing club data cannot be given
a chant.

@Y/<Chants>@
Compose chants and assign them to your
club or national team. Each can have up
to three songs, depending on the number
of supporters. You can also swap data
with friends by e-mail or Memory Card.

@Y/<Captain Selection>@
Choose the team captain. A strong
captain on the team makes it more
cohesive, so the players will perform
better in matches.

@Y/<National Team Chant>@
Choose the chant for the national team
from the songs in your save data or the
samples provided. This chant only takes
effect while you are the National Team
Manager.

@Y/<National Team Ground>@
This is the national team's training
ground. Run practical drills, check
tactics and make final adjustments
before a match. You can only enter the
ground when there is a national match.

@Y/<Sub Ground>@
Give instructions to the Youth Team,
which develops young players to fit the
club before they sign, and to the
Satellite squad, which holds and trains
six players outside the top team.

@Y/<Start Match>@
Play matches in the tournament format
you have set. These settings are saved
to the Dreamcast console, so when you
play the same tournament again, they
will be as you left them, saving you
the hassle of setting it up again.

@Y/<Swap>@
Swap players between the top team and
the Satellite squad. Foreign players
cannot be moved up if that would give
the top team five or more. Conversely,
nobody can go down if the top team
would fall below eight.

@Y/<Policy Orders>@
Set the Satellite policy and train them
for the future. If you need players who
can play now, pick the club's current
policy. If you are planning ahead, pick
a policy based on future tactics, with
younger players. Since they train from
a young age, physical development is
much greater.

@Y/<Formation>@
Select the Satellite formation policy.
Satellite players train to adapt to the
formation you choose.

@Y/<Tactics>@
Select the Satellite tactics policy.
Satellite players train to adapt to the
tactic you choose.

@Y/<Midfield Defence>@
Set the Satellite policy for midfield
defence: use the zonal press or not.
Satellite players train to adapt to the
policy you choose.

@Y/<DF Type>@
Set the Satellite DF type policy.
Satellite players train to adapt to the
DF type you choose.

@Y/<3-6-1>@
The Satellite squad will train to adapt
to the 3-6-1 formation. If it works,
you can expect great ball control in
midfield.

@Y/<4-5-1>@
The Satellite squad will train to adapt
to the 4-5-1 formation. If it works,
you can expect a very solid defence and
fast moves from defence into attack.

@Y/<5-4-1>@
The Satellite squad will train to adapt
to the 5-4-1 formation. It suits the
counter-attack well. If it works, they
can leave the opposition's defence
standing with a lightning counter.

@Y/<3-5-2>@
The Satellite squad will train to adapt
to the 3-5-2 formation. If it works,
they can switch quickly between attack
and defence and play a tight game.

@Y/<4-4-2>@
The Satellite squad will train to adapt
to the 4-4-2 formation. It can adapt
flexibly to attack and defence, so
expect solid, dependable matches.

@Y/<5-3-2>@
The Satellite squad will train to adapt
to the 5-3-2 formation. If it works,
it gives a solid defence that does not
let the opposition score. With few
midfielders, though, you should choose
attacking tactics that make good use of
the full-backs.

@Y/<4-3-3>@
The Satellite squad will train to adapt
to the 4-3-3 formation. If it works, it
becomes a formation that excels in both
attack and defence.

@Y/<3-4-3>@
The Satellite squad will train to adapt
to the 3-4-3 formation. If it works,
you can expect high scoring power.

@Y/<Hold-up Play>@
The Satellite squad will train to adapt
to the hold-up play tactic. If it
works, attacks in front of goal will be
more varied and goals should follow.

@Y/<Left Flank Attack>@
The Satellite squad will train to adapt
to the left flank attack tactic. If it
works, they can exploit the space on
the left and build their attacks.

@Y/<Right Flank Attack>@
The Satellite squad will train to adapt
to the right flank attack tactic. If it
works, they can exploit the space on
the right and build their attacks.

@Y/<Central Attack>@
The Satellite squad will train to adapt
to attacking through the middle. If it
works, they can take the shortest
route to goal.

@Y/<Counter-Attack>@
The Satellite squad will train to adapt
to the counter-attack tactic. If it
works, a solid defence lets them hit
quickly and score before opponents get
back.

@Y/<Normal>@
The Satellite squad will train to adapt
to normal midfield defence. With no
zonal press, midfielders tire less
quickly.

@Y/<Zonal Press>@
The Satellite squad will train to adapt
to the zonal press in midfield. If it
works, they can crowd out opponents,
win the ball and launch an attack.

@Y/<Line>@
The Satellite squad will train to adapt
to the Line defender type. If it
works, they can push the defensive line
up at once and catch opponents
offside.

@Y/<Libero>@
The Satellite squad will train to adapt
to the Libero defender type. If a
suitable player is there, they will
join the attack at the right moment, so
expect more attacking power.

@Y/<Sweeper>@
The Satellite squad will train to adapt
to the Sweeper type. If the squad has a
suitable Sweeper, they will cover gaps
in defence accurately and keep things
very tight at the back.

@Y/<To the Meeting Room>@
Head to the Meeting Room.

@Y/<To Data Room: Club Info>@
Head to Data Room: Club Info.

@Y/<To the Training Ground>@
Head to the training ground.
